title: Stand With the Boycott?
summary: DRAFT, not yet fact-checked. Your town must choose how strictly to enforce the boycott of British goods, without knowing what Britain will do next.

briefing.heading: A port closed
briefing.text: In 1774, Parliament punished Boston for the destruction of East India Company tea by closing its port. Other laws followed that changed how Massachusetts was governed. Many colonists saw these as an attack on their rights.

image.alt: A printed broadside from 1774, dense with small type, in which Boston's Committee of Correspondence responds to the closing of Boston's port.

briefing.heading: A colony-wide agreement
briefing.text: That October, delegates from twelve colonies signed the Continental Association. Starting December 1, 1774, the colonies would stop importing British goods. Merchants who kept selling them would be breaking the agreement.

image.alt: A 1774 print of a rearing black horse that has thrown its rider. The rider has hit his head on a mile marker reading "To Boston VI miles", and a signpost points toward Salem.

briefing.heading: Your town decides
briefing.text: The agreement told every town to elect a committee to watch who bought and sold British goods. Tonight your town meets to decide how strictly that committee will do its work. Nobody knows yet whether Britain will back down.

briefing.heading: Where you are
briefing.text: DRAFT, written by the CS team for review. This map of New England was printed in London in 1774. Your town is one of many small towns in Massachusetts. Boston, the port Parliament closed, is on the coast to the east.

image.alt: A hand-colored 1774 map of New England showing Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Connecticut and Rhode Island, with the Atlantic coast on the right.

marker.label: Your town is somewhere in Massachusetts

figures.name: Mr. Hale
figures.role: A shopkeeper who sells imported cloth and tea

figures.name: Mrs. Porter
figures.role: A member of the town's committee of inspection

figures.name: Mr. Bray
figures.role: A farmer who owes money at Mr. Hale's shop

merchant_intro.text: I have shelves of British cloth I paid for last summer. If I sell it, the committee may print my name in the newspaper. If I do not, I cannot pay what I owe.

choices.text: What happens if your name is printed?
Could you sell something else instead?
Do you think the boycott is right?

merchant_printed.text: Then every man who signed the agreement stops trading with me. Not only here. The newspapers travel. I have seen it happen to shopkeepers in Boston.

merchant_harsh.text: Harsh, perhaps. But they would say a boycott that nobody enforces is no boycott at all. I cannot say they are wrong. I only wish it were not my shelves.

merchant_alternative.text: Some families are spinning their own cloth now and wearing it proudly. That is well for them. It is not a trade I can start in a month with money already spent.

merchant_belief.text: I believe Parliament has gone too far. I also believe my children eat by what I sell. Both of those are true at once, and I have not found a way to make them agree.

committee_intro.text: The agreement is plain. Our committee watches who buys and sells, and we publish the name of anyone who breaks it. If towns go soft, Parliament learns we did not mean it.

choices.text: Isn't that hard on Mr. Hale?
What if you are wrong about someone?
What do you think Britain will do?

committee_hale.text: It is. I have known him twenty years. But if we excuse him, the next town excuses theirs, and soon the agreement is only words. What we have instead of an army is that we all hold to it.

committee_wrong.text: Then we have ruined a neighbor over a rumor. That worries me more than I say aloud. We meet, we hear the case, and we are careful. Careful is not the same as certain.

committee_britain.text: I do not know. Some say they will repeal the laws within the year. Others say soldiers. Anyone who tells you they know is guessing.

farmer_intro.text: I owe Hale for seed. If the committee ruins him, he calls in what I owe, and I have not got it. I care about the cause. I also care about spring planting.

choices.text: So what do you want the town to do?
Would you buy British goods anyway?

farmer_want.text: Something between. Let him sell what he already bought and buy nothing new. But I am a farmer, not a lawyer, and nobody at the meeting will ask me.

farmer_buy.text: And have my name in the paper? No. But I know men who would, quietly, and call it nobody's business.

decision.prompt: The town meeting is tonight. What do you vote for?
decision.context: You do not know whether Britain will repeal the laws, ignore the colonies, or send soldiers. You do know that your neighbors will remember how you voted.

options.text: Enforce the agreement strictly, and publish the names of anyone who breaks it
Let merchants sell goods they bought before December, but nothing new
Refuse to enforce the agreement in this town

outcome_strict.title: The town holds
outcome_strict.text: Your committee publishes two names that winter. Both shops lose customers, and one closes. Imports into the colonies fall sharply through 1775. Your town is counted among those that held firm, and some neighbors no longer speak to one another.

outcome_middle.title: A line that bends
outcome_middle.text: Mr. Hale sells his old stock and orders nothing new. Some townspeople call it sensible. Others say a rule with exceptions is not a rule, and ask who decides which goods are old.

outcome_refuse.title: Standing apart
outcome_refuse.text: Word travels that your town will not enforce the agreement. Under Article 14, colonies and towns that broke the Association risked being cut off from trade with everyone else. Merchants in neighboring towns grow reluctant to deal with yours.

reveal.text:
Committees of inspection were elected in towns across the colonies, exactly as the agreement asked. They did publish names. Newspapers printed lists of violators, and the pressure worked: British imports to the colonies collapsed in 1775.

Nobody voting in early 1775 knew that. They did not know Lexington and Concord were months away. People made the choice you just made without knowing how it ended, and reasonable neighbors chose differently from one another.

reflection.prompt: What did you wish you knew before you voted, that nobody in 1775 could have known?
Mr. Hale and Mrs. Porter both thought they were doing the right thing. What was each of them most afraid of?
Was there a choice here with no cost to anyone? What does that tell you about the decisions people faced?
